messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Bao, a 46-year-old software engineer, described his life as having been lived behind a wall of glass for the better part of two decades. The man his wife married was not the man who sat in the office today; that man, he felt, had died twenty years ago on a dusty road outside of Fallujah. The trauma was old, but its presence was constant. It began with the high-pitched whine of a motorcycle weaving through their convoy's traffic. Bao remembers the smell of hot dust and diesel exhaust just before the world dissolved into a deafening roar and a flash of white heat. He was thrown from the vehicle, his body battered but intact, yet trapped in the wreckage. The moments that followed are a slideshow of sensory horror he cannot articulate; the sounds of screaming, the metallic tang of blood, the acrid smell of burning rubber and explosives. It is this silent film that plays on a loop in his mind, a memory he can feel and hear but never seems to be able to put into words.

In the years that followed his return, the war came home with him. At first, the intrusions were infrequent, but they grew in power and scope. Any loud, sudden noise could be a threat, but the sound of a motorcycle engine was a direct portal back to the attack. Hearing one pass his suburban home would instantly trigger the memory, not as a thought, but as a full-body experience. The roar of the IED would fill his ears, and the silent film of the aftermath would begin its relentless replay. This constant re-experiencing convinced him that danger was not a memory but an imminent reality. His sense of threat became pervasive; he felt perpetually on guard, even within the supposed safety of his own home, checking locks and peering through blinds. Strangers on the street were no longer neutral figures but potential assailants, their approach causing a surge of panic that felt identical to the terror of that day.

This ever-present feeling of threat began to dictate the shape of his life. To feel safe, he had to control his environment, which meant shrinking it. He started by avoiding unfamiliar places, where he couldn't map out every potential danger. Soon, this bled into avoiding going out altogether, a retreat made easier by his job as a software engineer, which allowed him to work entirely from home. He reasoned that if he stayed inside, he couldn't be caught off guard. This avoidance, however, only amplified his hypervigilance. Confined to his house, his senses sharpened to any potential trigger that might breach his fortress. The scent of a neighbor's barbecue could take on the menacing quality of something burning, and his mind, starved of new input, would more readily slip back into the well-worn grooves of the traumatic memory. His strategies to suppress the past were paradoxically making it more present.

The cycle has become a prison of his own making. A trigger, like the motorcycle, ignites the memory and the overwhelming sense of threat. This feeling of imminent danger then justifies and deepens his avoidance strategies. He can’t watch action movies with his wife because the sounds of explosions are too real. He stopped exercising because the sensation of a pounding heart and rapid breathing felt too much like the physical precursors to death, which in turn could bring the memories flooding back. His avoidance has starved his life of any experience that might contradict his core belief that the world is fundamentally unsafe. By never leaving the house, he never learns that strangers are just people or that the neighborhood is peaceful. This lack of corrective experience strengthens his sense of threat, which makes him even more sensitive to triggers and more likely to be ambushed by the non-verbal horror of his memories. Even moments of supposed privacy are fraught; the vulnerability of being naked in the shower brings a specific terror of being exposed and helpless, just as he was in the wreckage.

Bao finally sought therapy after his wife told him, with tears in her eyes, that she felt she was losing him. His isolation had become a chasm between them. He sits in the therapy room, a man haunted by a war that ended for the world but never for him. He cannot find the words for what happened, but he is desperate to stop hearing its sounds and to finally step out from behind the glass and live in the world again, not just watch it pass by.
